name: METR (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: an AI catastrophe kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research, Berkeley) measures what frontier AI agents can do on their own and whether their developers could lose control of them: in 2024, its first year as a charity of its own, it evaluated GPT-4o, o1-preview and Claude 3.5 Sonnet before release with OpenAI and Anthropic, built task suites calibrated on human experts and RE-Bench for AI research and development, and analysed companies' frontier safety policies. This model covers its one programme in 2024 ($6.9M of $8.2M spent). At the defaults it averts about 0.05 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.003 to 0.4 in 90% of the simulation's draws, so the result is mostly uncertainty: each dollar is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate. It is under a tenth of its cause's median, close to Redwood Research's and MIRI's, because all its work is against AI escaping its developers' control, and Rethink's typical misalignment project cuts the deaths in catastrophes the world survives far less per dollar than its typical misuse project, which carries most of FAR.AI's and the Center for AI Safety's results; the next dollar counts at 28% of the past average because commitments of about $71M arrived in 2026, and a tenth of the value is taken off for evaluations speeding the race. The chance of an AI catastrophe (the slider), the typical cut per dollar, the discount rate and the share of work counted as misuse (0 by default; counting its cybersecurity tasks as misuse work, 10%, would raise the result nine times) are the biggest swings; the one branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

rows.label: AI: share of the AI spending on work against misuse (dangerous-capability evaluations, defences against misuse)
rows.explainer: The share of METR's AI spending that is work against misuse. None of its 2024 work is aimed at misuse: its evaluations and research measure whether AI agents can act autonomously (copy themselves, do AI research and development, run long tasks without help), the capabilities by which developers could lose control of them ('whether their developers could lose control of them', its about page), and its partner in the Audacious grant, RAND, took the misuse side ('RAND's parallel work on evaluating AI systems focuses primarily on assessing the potential for their misuse'). Some of its tasks are cybersecurity tasks (HCAST: 189 tasks in machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, software engineering and general reasoning), but they measure an agent's general autonomy, not uplift to an attacker: work aimed at both counts as misalignment (the template's rule), so 0, our judgment, as for Redwood Research and MIRI. The high end, 10%, is the reading that the cybersecurity tasks are misuse work: one of HCAST's four domains, a smaller part of the effort than the AI research and development tasks of RE-Bench. FAR.AI's 28% and the Center for AI Safety's 25% are for jailbreak and hazardous-knowledge work.

How far the typical project's effect applies to this charity's work
rows.explainer: METR's work against Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project. Above typical, by the template's test (evaluations labs or governments run): in 2024 it evaluated GPT-4o, o1-preview and Claude 3.5 Sonnet before release in partnership with OpenAI and Anthropic (its risk-assessment page), one of the few groups outside the companies and governments' AI safety institutes with such access; it is partnering with the UK AI Security Institute, gives technical help to the European AI Office and is a member of NIST's AI Safety Institute Consortium (about page); its task suites and RE-Bench (November 2024) became the measures others report. Below in how directly it acts: no 2024 model crossed a threshold, so no evaluation changed a release, and its findings bind no one. 1.2, our judgment, the family's upper bound for a best guess, as for FAR.AI's, the Center for AI Safety's and Redwood's research (1.2); the range 0.5 to 2.5, as Redwood's, its high end for labs running its evaluations on their own models before release, its low end for evaluations that change no decision; wide because whether an evaluation changes a decision is unobserved.

rows.label: Share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: The share of the work no one else would have done now: the UK and US AI safety institutes tested frontier models before release in 2024 too, Apollo Research evaluates scheming, and the companies' own teams run dangerous-capability evaluations, so some of METR's evaluations would have been done by others; its measures of autonomy on human-calibrated tasks (time taken by human experts) had no close substitute. Our judgment, 0.65 (0.35 to 0.85), as for FAR.AI and the Center for AI Safety; that the work would have come later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: METR's share of all resources behind its evaluations: the companies give it model access before release, their staff's time and free tokens ('These companies have also provided access and tokens, which we use for evaluations, research, and engineering', about page), none of which is in its accounts; METR's own cloud computing was $1.09M in 2024 (Part IX line 14). No fees (program service revenue $0, Part I line 9). 0.7, our judgment, 0.5 to 0.9, between Redwood's research (0.65, whose largest result was a joint paper with a lab) and FAR.AI's and MIRI's 0.85: the work is METR's own but runs on the companies' models and tokens.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted: its measures of AI agents' abilities inform governments and the public about AI progress generally (the EU AI Office's technical assistance, the time-horizon measure built on its 2024 task suites), and its evaluations also guard against harms smaller than a catastrophe (an agent misbehaving inside a lab). 10% (0 to 30%) of the modelled value, our judgment, as for FAR.AI, the Center for AI Safety and Redwood Research.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): METR's are dangerous-capability evaluations, the template's example of work clearly riskier than typical. A report finding no dangerous capability can make a release look safe without bounding what the model can do; its benchmarks of AI research and development (RE-Bench) and of long tasks give developers targets to improve on, and its trend lines feed the race and the investment behind it. -10%, our judgment, -30% to 0, the low end of the template's band for dangerous-capability evaluations (-0.1 to -0.3), because its threat model is autonomy rather than uplift, and twice Redwood's and the Center for AI Safety's -5%.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: METR publishes how well agents do on autonomy tasks and how it elicits their abilities (agent scaffolds, task suites), which shows little to a bad actor about weapons but some to anyone building autonomous agents; it keeps most task details private against contamination. -2%, down to -10%, our judgment, as for Redwood Research, below FAR.AI's -5% for working attacks on safeguards.
